title: The Tetris effect
hook: Play enough Tetris and you start seeing falling blocks when you close your eyes.
peek: After long sessions of Tetris, many players see falling pieces as they drift off to sleep, or catch themselves fitting real objects together in their heads. Researchers have studied it seriously.
lede: Play Tetris for hours and something odd can happen. You close your eyes at night and the pieces keep falling. Walking down the street, you notice how the buildings would slot together. The name was popularised by a 1994 Wired article, and scientists have since used the game to study how the brain replays what it has been practising.

bullets.text: The journalist Jeffrey Goldsmith wrote about players who kept seeing blocks after long sessions, in dreams and in the shapes of the world around them. The name caught on from there.

In 2000, the Harvard sleep researcher had people play Tetris for several days. Many reported seeing falling pieces as they drifted off, and some experienced players saw pieces from older versions they had played years before.
The study also included a few people with amnesia. They could not remember playing the game, yet some of them still described falling, rotating blocks as they fell asleep.
These pictures on the edge of sleep are common. Stickgold's work suggested the brain may be replaying recent practice while memories settle, even when we cannot recall the practice itself.
